ety.text: From Middle English duracioun, from late Old French duracion, from Medieval Latin dūrātiō.

senses.d: An amount of time or a particular time interval.
ex: The duration of the flight will be about 2 hours 45 minutes.
She was moaning for the entire duration of the advert break.

senses.d: The time taken for the current situation to end, especially the current war.
ex: Rationing will last at least for the duration.

senses.d: A measure of the sensitivity of the price of a financial asset to changes in interest rates, computed for a simple bond as a weighted average of the maturities of the interest and principal payments associated with it.

ety.text: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dūrātiōnem, from Latin dūrō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dūrātiōnem. By surface analysis, durar + -ção.
From Middle English during, durynge, durinde, durand, durende, present participle of duren (“to last”), equivalent to dure + -ing. Compare Dutch gedurende (“during”). More at dure.

senses.d: For all of a given time interval; throughout; in; pending.
ex: I lived with my parents during the 1970s.
This shop, which was among the few able to stay open during the war, is closed during the whole of August.

senses.d: At any time or period within a given time interval or while a given event is ongoing.
ex: I lived with my parents at several points during the 1980s.
Many of the best examples were produced during the Restoration.

ety.text: From Latin dūrantem (“enduring”), from dūrō (“last, endure”), from dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *deru-, *drew- (“hard, fest”).
From Middle English durable, from Old French durable, from Latin dūrābilis (“lasting, permanent”), from dūrō (“harden, make hard”).

senses.d: Able to resist wear or decay; lasting; enduring.
ex: Near-synonyms: persistent, long-lasting, lasting, hard-wearing; see also Thesaurus:lasting

senses.d: A durable thing, one useful over more than one period, especially a year.
ex: In a frictionless world with perfect rental markets, there is an unambiguous cost associated with the use of a durable for a single period.

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin dūrābilis. Morphologically, from durer + -able.

pt:durável.gl: durable (able to resist decay; lasting; enduring)

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin dūrābilis. By surface analysis, durar + -ável.
